entries.title: daemon: add a --once flag to run one cycle and exit
entries.body:
Add a `--once` CLI flag to `agentflow.daemon`: when passed, run a single
`cycle(REPOS)` and exit, instead of entering the poll loop. Useful for testing the
pipeline end-to-end without the persistent daemon or the enable flag.

**Acceptance**
- `uv run python -m agentflow.daemon --once` runs exactly one cycle (one issue per
  repo) and exits 0.
- Without `--once`, the existing dormant-by-default poll loop is unchanged.
- `--once` is an explicit manual run, so it bypasses the enable-flag gate (like an
  on-demand run) but still respects the single-instance lock.

Keep it minimal; add/extend a test in `tests/test_daemon.py` if it fits.

entries.title: dashboard pools widget: distinguish dispatch budget from rate-limit headroom
entries.body:
## Summary

The dashboard **Pools / "rate-limit headroom"** widget headlines the wrong ceiling.
It shows headroom against the **rate-limit ceiling (100%)** while the `busy` flag is
decided against the **40% autonomous-dispatch cap** — so the two halves of the pill
disagree. Live example right now:

```
claude   14% headroom · busy
codex    34% headroom · busy   (amber bar)
```

"34% headroom · busy" reads as a contradiction: plenty of headroom, yet busy. As a
*dispatch* signal it's misleading.

## Why it's wrong

Two different ceilings are spliced into one pill:

- **Headroom shown** = `100 - spent_pct` — distance to the rate-limit ceiling.
  `agentflow/dashboard_data.py:24`.
- **`busy`/`clear`** = the gate `check` (`balancer._query_pool`, `agentflow/balancer.py:76`),
  which blocks when `spent ≥ THRESHOLD_PCT` (default **40**, `triage-gate.sh:66/:421`).

So codex at 66% spend → `headroom_pct = 34`, but `clear = False` because 66 ≥ 40. The
number on screen is the one quantity that *doesn't* govern dispatch.

### Three concrete defects

1. **Wrong number headlined.** The widget shows interactive headroom (vs 100), not
   dispatch budget (vs the 40% cap). `dashboard_data.py:24`.
2. **Color anchored to the wrong ceiling.** `headroomColor = h>40 ? green : h>15 ? amber : red`
   is applied to the 100-based headroom (`agentflow/static/dashboard.html:197`), so codex
   at 34 renders **amber** ("eh, fine") while it's 26 points *over* the dispatch cap and
   fully blocked.
3. **`busy` hides its cause.** codex `busy` = over the 40% spend cap; claude `busy` =
   "a session was active in the last 10m". Same word, different reasons, neither surfaced
   (`dashboard.html:302-307`).

## Impact

This widget's stated job is the **"idle while queued = bug"** signal
(`agentflow/dashboard_data.py:19`). As rendered, an operator sees "34% headroom, amber"
with issues queued and concludes the fleet is broken or wasting capacity — when the gate
is actually doing its job. The widget shows the one quantity that doesn't decide dispatch,
producing exactly that false alarm.

## Suggested direction (not prescriptive)

- Headline **dispatch budget vs the 40% cap**, not raw headroom-to-ceiling.
- Plumb the threshold into `PoolStatus` / `pools()` — it isn't in the snapshot today
  (`PoolStatus` carries only `tool/clear/spent_pct`).
- Draw the **reserve line** (the 40% cap) on the bar; color by `clear`, not by
  `headroomColor(h)`.
- Make `busy` state its reason (over-cap vs recently-active).

## Charter note

The rendering change is a **UI change → must go through `/ui-mockups` to a locked visual
spec before build** (engineering charter; `mockups/dashboard-inbox.html` is the current
locked spec, must honor `PRODUCT.md`/`DESIGN.md`). The data-plumbing half (threshold into
the snapshot) is non-UI. **Not `ready-for-agent` until the widget has a locked mockup.**

entries.title: intake: land the Agent Brief in the issue body so build and review actually use it
entries.body:
## Summary

The entire intake stage's output is invisible to the pipeline it feeds. Intake grounds an issue and writes an Agent Brief, but posts it as an issue **comment** — while the builder's prompt and the reviewer's acceptance anchor both read the issue **body**, i.e. the raw, pre-intake text. ADR 0016 ("rewrites the title and description") and ADR 0022 ("the frozen scope intake writes into the issue body") both already specify body.

## Verified

- `apply_intake` (agentflow/intake.py) posts the brief with `gh issue comment` and never edits the body.
- `run_once` (agentflow/loop.py) fills `BUILD_PROMPT`'s `{body}` from `issue.get("body")`; `_build_review_merge` sets `acceptance = issue.get("body") or ""` for the reviewer.
- Field evidence (ciq-autotune): briefs with grounded numbers (e.g. #302's "median pre-meal BG 155 across 38 meals") sat in comments while the build ran from the original one-line body.

## Current behavior

On `route=ready` the brief is a 3–8 KB comment; the body stays as filed; builder and reviewer consume the vague original. The comment also doubles as the thread reply the maintainer reads — a report wall instead of a conversation.

## Desired behavior

On `route=ready` (daemon and `/agentflow` verbs alike — both go through `apply_intake`):

1. Write the brief **into the issue body**, preserving the as-filed text under a collapsed `<details>` block at the bottom.
2. Post a **short conversational comment** instead of the wall (2–5 sentences: what was verified, that the brief now lives in the description), still starting with the intake disclaimer line.
3. `grill` / `mockup` routes keep posting comments — those are conversations, not build inputs.

## Key interfaces

`apply_intake` in agentflow/intake.py is the single write path — explore fresh; pointers, not line numbers. Traps: the retitle path prepends a `Retitled from:` note to the comment (keep it); the resume machinery keys on the intake marker in comments (keep the marker discipline); a **re-intake on resume must update the body brief in place**, not append a second brief.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] After a ready routing, the issue body IS the Agent Brief, with the original preserved under `<details>`.
- [ ] `BUILD_PROMPT` and the reviewer's acceptance receive the brief content with no further loop changes (they already read the body).
- [ ] The thread comment on ready is short (≤ ~8 lines), conversational, and carries the disclaimer marker.
- [ ] A resume/re-intake updates the existing body brief rather than appending a second one.
- [ ] Pure test: the body-composition helper (brief + `<details>`-wrapped original), including the update-in-place case.
- [ ] `skills/agentflow/SKILL.md` "Land it as ready" describes the same body-write behavior.

## Out of scope

Comment idempotence and the no-spam resume route (tracked separately); grill/mockup comment shape.

entries.title: review gate: make the UI screenshot requirement mechanical and unwaivable
entries.body:
## Summary

The charter's UI-evidence gate (before/after screenshots on any user-facing change) exists only as prompt text, and reviewers waive it. It must become mechanical: a PR that touches a declared UI surface and carries no image cannot pass the gate, regardless of what the reviewer says.

## Verified

- Field evidence (ciq-autotune, post-enrollment): **1 of 8** UI PRs carried screenshots. PR #338 (Guide KB) merged unseen and was reverted 19 minutes later — the human's first look at pixels was production. The reviewer on PR #352 explicitly downgraded the charter gate to a nit ("PHI-justified… not blocking") — the PHI excuse is solved (sibling PRs used scratch DBs). A dark-mode contrast regression (#349) shipped because nothing captures dark mode.
- `BUILD_PROMPT` and `REVIEW_PROMPT` state the gate; `REVISE_PROMPT` (agentflow/loop.py) carries neither evidence gate, so a revise pass can degrade compliance.
- The "user-facing surface" definition is a hardcoded example (`e.g. frontend/`) inside the reviewer prompt — it doesn't even match this repo's own UI (`agentflow/static/`).

## Desired behavior

1. **Per-repo surface declaration**: a `ui-surfaces:` line in the repo's AGENTS.md next to `profile:` (e.g. `ui-surfaces: frontend/, agentflow/static/`), parsed the same way as the profile.
2. **Mechanical check, independent of the review verdict**: changed files ∩ declared surfaces ≠ ∅ AND no image in the PR body or comments → the PR cannot auto-merge and parks with a plain-language reason. The reviewer cannot waive it.
3. The declared surfaces feed `BUILD_PROMPT`/`REVIEW_PROMPT` in place of the hardcoded example.
4. `REVISE_PROMPT` carries both evidence gates (screenshots + plain-language body).
5. Where the app has light and dark themes, screenshots cover both.

## Key interfaces

`decide_merge`/`park` (agentflow/gate.py) for the mechanical check; the AGENTS.md fact parsing near `repo_profile` (agentflow/loop.py); the three prompts. Trap: image detection must accept both markdown images and GitHub user-asset URLs.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A PR touching a declared surface with no image attached cannot auto-merge and parks with the reason, even on a clean review.
- [ ] The check runs independent of (after) the review verdict — a reviewer "not blocking" cannot clear it.
- [ ] Surfaces are read per repo from AGENTS.md; this repo declares `agentflow/static/`.
- [ ] `REVISE_PROMPT` names both evidence gates.
- [ ] Pure tests: the surface-intersection predicate and the image-presence detector.

## Out of scope

Pixel-diffing the screenshots against the locked mockup (worth a follow-up ADR); requiring screenshots on non-UI changes.

entries.title: parked PRs: answer maintainer comments, and an open question blocks the merge path
entries.body:
## Summary

Once a PR parks for human review, the pipeline never looks at it again — maintainer comments on it go unanswered. A question from the human who merges must get an answer, and while it's unanswered nothing should merge autonomously.

## Verified

- Field evidence (ciq-autotune PR #351): the maintainer asked "Show me a screenshot please?" on a parked PR; no agent ever replied, and the PR was merged four hours later with the request unanswered.
- `gate.park` posts the park comment and that's the last touch; the per-cycle work (agentflow/loop.py) is one intake + one build — no parked-PR pass. The held-**issue** resume path exists (`awaiting_recheck`); there is no PR sibling.

## Desired behavior

Each daemon cycle, for open agentflow PRs whose latest comment is the maintainer's (reuse the marker discipline to tell ours apart), spawn a responder session in the PR-branch worktree that:

- answers the question conversationally in a PR comment (marker-prefixed),
- attaches requested evidence (e.g. runs the screenshot pass when asked),
- pushes small fixes to the **same branch** when that's what was asked — same contract as revise: never a new PR, never a merge.

On `autonomous` repos, an unanswered maintainer comment **blocks auto-merge** until addressed.

## Key interfaces

The park/revise machinery in agentflow/loop.py and agentflow/gate.py; the comment-marker conventions in agentflow/intake.py. Traps: don't wake on our own park/revise comments; this is a reply, not a fresh review — answer what was asked.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A maintainer comment on a parked PR gets an in-thread, marker-prefixed reply within one cycle.
- [ ] A screenshot request on a repo with a UI results in an attached screenshot.
- [ ] `autonomous`: auto-merge is blocked while the latest maintainer comment is unanswered — pure predicate test.
- [ ] The responder never merges and never opens a new PR.

## Out of scope

Re-running full review on every comment; notification changes.

entries.title: runner: every subprocess gets a timeout; the CI watch is bounded
entries.body:
## Summary

No subprocess anywhere in the pipeline has a timeout. One hung tool session or a stuck CI watch freezes the single-threaded daemon indefinitely — and with it the lock heartbeat, which after the 3-hour stale threshold invites a second daemon (whose claim-reclaim would then duplicate live work).

## Verified

- `_run` (agentflow/runner.py) calls `subprocess.run` with no timeout; every `gh`/`git`/session launch goes through it or a sibling.
- `ci_is_green` (agentflow/gate.py) uses `gh pr checks --watch` — unbounded on a stuck check.
- The daemon heartbeats its lock only at cycle top (agentflow/daemon.py), so a frozen cycle freezes the heartbeat too.

## Desired behavior

- `_run` takes a timeout (default generous, env-tunable) — one choke point, not scattered per-call values.
- Session launches get a long ceiling (e.g. `AGENTFLOW_SESSION_TIMEOUT`, default ~2h).
- The CI wait becomes a bounded poll (deadline + interval; default ~30 min) instead of `--watch`.
- A timed-out build classifies as `INCOMPLETE` and follows the existing stuck-build handback (draft-PR preservation + held issue). A timed-out `gh` read is a failure → the existing fail-closed paths.

## Key interfaces

`runner._run` (deepen it — the timeout is part of its contract); `gate.ci_is_green`. Trap: `subprocess.TimeoutExpired` must be classified, never allowed to propagate and kill the daemon loop.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] No unbounded subprocess call remains under `agentflow/`.
- [ ] A simulated hang (test with a sleep beyond a tiny timeout) classifies as incomplete/failed instead of blocking.
- [ ] The CI wait returns not-green at its deadline — test the bounded poll.

## Out of scope

The lock/heartbeat redesign (its own issue); parallel dispatch.

entries.title: daemon: stale-lock reclaim takes real ownership; the heartbeat survives long cycles
entries.body:
## Summary

Two single-instance bugs in the daemon lock. Single-instance is load-bearing: the dispatch claims are check-then-set and assume exactly one daemon (ADR 0021) — a second live daemon can strip a live claim and duplicate a build.

## Verified

- On a stale lock (>3h), `_acquire_lock` (agentflow/daemon.py) returns True **without recreating or claiming the lock dir** — two simultaneous starters can both "reclaim" and run concurrently, and either's shutdown (`finally: LOCK.rmdir()`) removes the other's lock.
- The heartbeat (`os.utime`) fires only at cycle top. A cycle longer than the 3-hour stale threshold — one slow build+review+revise chain across four repos is realistic — makes a *healthy* daemon look stale.

## Desired behavior

- Stale reclaim takes real ownership: remove + atomically recreate the lock, write the owner pid inside.
- Shutdown removes the lock only if this process owns it (pid check).
- The heartbeat survives long cycles: a background thread touching the lock every ~60s, or a staleness threshold sized far above the worst-case cycle with the invariant documented.

## Key interfaces

`_acquire_lock` / `main` in agentflow/daemon.py — keep it a deep module: acquire/heartbeat/release as one small lock seam. Trap: the reclaim race itself (two starters removing + recreating) — mkdir is the atomic step; exactly one may win.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Test: two acquirers racing a stale lock — exactly one proceeds.
- [ ] Test: shutdown does not remove a lock owned by another pid.
- [ ] A cycle longer than the stale threshold no longer lets a second daemon in (heartbeat thread, or raised threshold + documented invariant).

## Out of scope

Subprocess timeouts (separate issue); multi-daemon/parallel dispatch.

entries.title: loop: a failed merge parks and pings instead of silently idling
entries.body:
## Summary

When the final squash-merge fails (branch protection, a new conflict, a transient GitHub error), the pipeline logs one line and moves on: no park comment, no ping, no ratchet record. The PR sits open — the issue is skipped by the open-PR dedup — until the human happens to browse past it. Every other terminal state pings; this one is a silent wedge.

## Verified

The merge-failure path in `_build_review_merge` (agentflow/loop.py) returns a "merge failed" string without calling `park`/`notify`/`ratchet.record`; compare the park path right next to it, which does all three.

## Desired behavior

On merge failure: park the PR with a plain-language reason (what failed), send the needs-you ping, and record a ratchet event — the same treatment as any other handback.

## Key interfaces

`_build_review_merge` merge branch (agentflow/loop.py); `gate.park`; `notify`. Trap: keep the park comment's finding-list format machine-parseable (the `/agentflow revise` verb reads it) — a merge failure has no findings, so the plain-language lede carries the reason.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A failed merge produces a park comment + notify + ratchet record — test with a monkeypatched merge.
- [ ] The success path is unchanged.

## Out of scope

Retrying the merge; conflict auto-resolution (ADR 0009 owns merge-time collision policy).

entries.title: interactive surface: claim triaging in manual verbs, real labels in the snippet, repo-arg entrypoint (ADR 0022 leftovers)
entries.body:
## Summary

PR #14 landed the core of ADR 0022 (the frozen work order is gone, `build_issue`/`build <N>` exists, `BUILD_PROMPT` names the charter test standard). Three drift items from the original scope remain — all in the interactive surface and the loop entrypoint.

## Verified (post-#14)

- `skills/agentflow/SKILL.md`'s "Land it as ready" snippet still passes the literal `current_labels=[]`. Copied verbatim on a held issue it leaves `ready-for-agent` AND the hold label both set — the daemon then both builds it and treats it as resumable (a re-triage of an issue already building).
- The manual verbs (`triage`/`pickup`/`scope`) never set the `agentflow:triaging` claim — the exact manual-race gap ADR 0021's consequences call out ("a manual `/agentflow` triage racing the daemon… posts a duplicate intake summary").
- `python -m agentflow.loop`'s `__main__` is still hardcoded to `ConnorGriffin/agentflow-sandbox` — running it from any other enrolled repo drives the pipeline against the wrong repo.

## Desired behavior

1. The SKILL.md snippet fetches the issue's real labels (`gh issue view N --json labels`) and passes them, so a promotion clears the hold label.
2. `triage`/`pickup`/`scope` claim `agentflow:triaging` before their grounding/grilling work and release it when the state label lands — mirroring the daemon's `_claim_triage`/`_release_triage`.
3. `__main__` takes the repo (and workdir) from argv; no hardcoded default repo.

## Key interfaces

skills/agentflow/SKILL.md; `_claim_triage`/`_release_triage` and `__main__` in agentflow/loop.py. Trap: the skill's claim must be released even when the human abandons the session — say so in the skill text (release on landing OR on giving up).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] SKILL.md snippet passes real labels; following it verbatim on a held issue leaves exactly one state label.
- [ ] SKILL.md instructs claiming/releasing `agentflow:triaging` around manual grounding.
- [ ] `python -m agentflow.loop <owner/repo> [workdir]` runs that repo; no sandbox default.
- [ ] Test: entrypoint argument parsing.

## Out of scope

Everything PR #14 already shipped (work order removal, `build <N>`, prompt hardening); the dotfiles `enroll` skill wording (different repo).

entries.title: intake: no-spam — a nothing-new recheck posts nothing, infra failures retry silently, comments are idempotent
entries.body:
## Summary

Three comment-spam vectors in intake, all violating ADR 0019's explicit "re-posts only if something genuinely remains open — no spam" promise. Field evidence: twin near-identical ~5 KB intake walls 39 seconds apart (ciq-autotune #337) and the same state restated three times (#277).

## Verified

- Every resume MUST post: `IntakeResult` requires a non-empty body and `apply_intake` posts it unconditionally — there is no "nothing to add" route, so a chit-chat maintainer reply on a held issue forces another full wall.
- An infra failure (worktree/provision error, launch non-zero — e.g. a rate-limit blip) returns the same `_held(...)` shape as a genuine model-level hold: it posts the "I couldn't ground this" comment and stamps `needs-grilling`, consuming the issue's state; each failed retry posts again.
- `apply_intake` has no idempotence guard — nothing checks whether the latest comment is already ours saying the same thing.

## Desired behavior

1. **A NOTHING_NEW route**: on resume, the session may answer "nothing genuinely open changed" → `apply_intake` is a no-op (no comment, labels unchanged).
2. **Infra failures retry silently**: distinguish session/worktree/launch failures from model-level holds; on infra failure post nothing, change no labels, and leave the issue for the next cycle. Bounded: after N consecutive failures on the same issue, post exactly one held comment.
3. **Idempotent apply**: `apply_intake` skips posting when the latest issue comment is ours with materially the same route + body.

## Key interfaces

`Intake.intake`, `parse_intake`, `apply_intake` (agentflow/intake.py). Trap: keep the fail-safe philosophy — an unparseable *decision* still holds for a human; only *infrastructure* failures become silent retries.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A resume with nothing new posts zero new comments (test).
- [ ] A worktree/launch failure posts no comment, changes no labels, and leaves the issue untriaged (test).
- [ ] Re-applying an identical result is a no-op (test).
- [ ] The N-consecutive-failure backstop posts exactly one held comment.

## Out of scope

Moving the brief into the issue body (its own issue); the resume author-allowlist (its own issue).

entries.title: loop: maintainer replies resume needs-mockup issues too
entries.body:
## Summary

The comment-resume path only watches `needs-grilling`; a maintainer reply on a `needs-mockup` issue does nothing. The mockup queue therefore stalls forever — in ciq-autotune, every issue parked at needs-mockup (#276, #277, #332) has sat untouched since enrollment with zero mockups produced. The loop's docstring also points at a verb that doesn't exist ("`/agentflow mockup`" — mockup entry actually lives under `pickup`).

## Verified

- `_next_resumable_issue` (agentflow/loop.py) queries only the `agentflow:needs-grilling` label.
- The same function's docstring names `/agentflow mockup`; `skills/agentflow/SKILL.md` has no such verb.

## Desired behavior

- Resume watches **both** hold labels. A reply on a mockup-held issue re-intakes with the reply as context — it may promote to ready (e.g. the maintainer waived the mockup or pointed at a locked spec) or sharpen what's still needed, same contract as grilling resume.
- Fix the docstring (and any other stale references) so `pickup` is named as the interactive mockup entry.

## Key interfaces

`_next_resumable_issue` (agentflow/loop.py), `awaiting_recheck` (agentflow/intake.py — unchanged, it's label-agnostic). Trap: the intake resume prompt currently assumes grilling-answer semantics; the mockup-held resume needs wording that allows "maintainer waived/locked the design" as a promotion path.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A reply on a `needs-mockup` issue is picked up on the next cycle — test the selector predicate over both labels.
- [ ] A waiver reply ("skip the mockup, build it") promotes to ready with dials, matching the grilling-resume shape.
- [ ] Docstring and SKILL.md agree: `pickup` is the mockup entry.

## Out of scope

Whether the daemon should *produce* mockups autonomously — that's a product decision, held separately.

entries.title: intake: quote-reply-safe resume detection and a maintainer allowlist
entries.body:
## Summary

Two related resume-detection gaps. (1) The marker match is a bare substring scan, so a GitHub **quote-reply** — which copies our disclaimer line into the maintainer's comment — makes their answer read as *our* comment: the issue silently never resumes, and the reply-extraction truncates their text. (2) There is no author check anywhere: **any** commenter (drive-by user, bot) whose comment lacks the marker triggers a full unattended grounding session seeded with their text — on any public repo that is a prompt-injection door into a permissions-bypassed session.

## Verified

- `awaiting_recheck` / `replies_since_intake` (agentflow/intake.py) match the intake marker as a substring anywhere in the comment body — a `> *agentflow intake…*` quoted line trips it.
- Neither the resume path nor intake dispatch filters by comment author.

## Desired behavior

1. Strip `>`-quoted lines from a comment before scanning for the marker, so quoting us still counts as a maintainer reply.
2. Resume (and any comment-triggered re-intake) fires only for comments from an **allowlisted author** — default the repo owner, extensible via a fact line in the repo's AGENTS.md. Comments from anyone else are inert: no session, no reply, no state change.

## Key interfaces

`awaiting_recheck`, `replies_since_intake` (agentflow/intake.py) — both pure, both tested; the comment JSON already carries author login (`gh … --json comments`). Trap: keep the functions pure — author allowlist arrives as a parameter, config parsing lives with the other AGENTS.md fact parsing.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A maintainer quote-reply of an intake comment counts as awaiting-recheck, and their full text survives extraction (pure tests).
- [ ] A non-allowlisted author's comment triggers no session and no state change (predicate test).
- [ ] The allowlist defaults to the repo owner and reads extra names from the repo's AGENTS.md facts.

## Out of scope

Sandboxing the sessions themselves; public-repo enrollment policy.

entries.title: runner: never adopt a dead PR or a stale worktree on re-build
entries.body:
## Summary

Re-running an issue can adopt a corpse. The branch→PR lookup matches PRs in **any** state, so a reopened issue (or a recurring title slug) classifies an old merged/closed PR as "opened" and the loop proceeds to review a dead PR. Reused worktrees keep their previous branch state instead of starting from origin/main, and worktrees of merged PRs are never pruned.

## Verified

- `_pr_for_branch` (agentflow/runner.py) passes `--state all` and takes the first match.
- `prepare_worktree` reuses an existing worktree/local branch as-is — no reset onto `origin/main` when there is no open PR.
- `.agentflow/worktrees/` accumulates one directory per build, forever.

## Desired behavior

- Match **open** PRs only (or compare PR created-at against the session start) so a dead PR never classifies a build as PR-opened.
- When reusing a worktree whose branch has no open PR, hard-reset it onto `origin/main` first.
- Prune worktrees whose PR has merged or closed (a daemon-cycle sweep).

## Key interfaces

`_pr_for_branch`, `prepare_worktree` (agentflow/runner.py); the daemon cycle for the sweep. Trap: never prune a worktree with an OPEN PR or uncommitted/unpushed work — the draft-PR handback path depends on stuck worktrees surviving.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A closed/merged PR on the branch → the build classifies as no-PR (the stuck-build handback), not PR-opened (test the classification).
- [ ] A reused worktree with no open PR starts from origin/main.
- [ ] The sweep removes only worktrees whose PR merged/closed and which are clean — test the predicate.

## Out of scope

Parallel builds; branch-name collision policy beyond the slug convention.

entries.title: labels: clean transitions — stale dials cleared on re-route, queue labels dropped on close
entries.body:
## Summary

Phase labels accrete instead of transitioning, and enrolled repos carry two parallel hold vocabularies. Closed issues wear contradictory queue labels, and a re-routed issue can end up with two complexity labels — with the loop silently picking whichever it matches first.

## Verified

- `apply_intake` (agentflow/intake.py) clears only the three state labels — never stale `agentflow:complexity:*` / `agentflow:effort:*` dials, so a re-route with different dials leaves both generations on the issue.
- Nothing strips queue/claim labels when an issue closes. Field evidence (ciq-autotune): #330 closed carrying `ready-for-agent` AND `needs-triage`; #331/#333/#295/#302 closed with `ready-for-agent` plus a pre-enrollment hold label.
- Two vocabularies live side-by-side in ciq-autotune: bare `needs-grilling`/`needs-mockup` (pre-enrollment) and `agentflow:needs-*` — issue #332 wears a different phase in each.

## Desired behavior

1. `apply_intake` clears stale dial labels when stamping new dials — an issue always has exactly one complexity and one effort label.
2. The merge path strips `ready-for-agent` (and any claim labels) from the issue it closes.
3. `enroll` gains an idempotent one-time sweep that maps legacy bare `needs-*` labels to the `agentflow:*` vocabulary (or removes them), reporting what it changed — one vocabulary per repo afterward.

## Key interfaces

`apply_intake` / `intake_labels` (agentflow/intake.py); the merge path in agentflow/loop.py; the enroll flow's label step. Trap: `ready-for-agent` stays bare by decision (ADR 0018) — the sweep must not rename it.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Re-routing to different dials leaves exactly one complexity and one effort label (test).
- [ ] A merged issue ends with no queue or claim labels.
- [ ] The sweep is idempotent and prints a summary of what it changed.

## Out of scope

Renaming `ready-for-agent` (settled, ADR 0018); GitHub Projects/board integration.

entries.title: review pipeline: run every cross-review at deep complexity
entries.body:
> *agentflow intake — generated by AI.*

## Summary

Run every cross-review with the deep model tier, while continuing to size builders from each issue's complexity dial. The maintainer accepted this policy choice after the earlier hold.

## Verified

- The premise holds: the reviewer currently resolves its model from the issue complexity passed into the review interface. A `standard` issue therefore launches a `standard` reviewer, while a `deep` issue launches a `deep` reviewer.
- There are exactly 2 supported complexity values: `standard` and `deep`. Today their builder/reviewer pairings are `standard`/`standard` and `deep`/`deep`; the desired pairings are `standard`/`deep` and `deep`/`deep`.
- Initial review, review after revision, and autonomous-survivor re-review all pass through the same Reviewer module, so the policy can be enforced at one interface rather than separately in each orchestration branch.
- The runner adapters already map `deep` to Opus for Claude and Sol for Codex. No new model mapping is required.
- The recorded sizing decision currently says review tracks issue complexity, so the decision documentation must be amended. The later two-dial decision changed the taxonomy but did not replace that reviewer-sizing behavior.
- This checkout declares no read-only production-data pull. The cited ciq-autotune incidents and fleet-wide cost estimate therefore cannot be independently counted here; they remain the policy rationale supplied in the issue.

## Current behavior

A standard issue uses a Sonnet/Terra-class builder and a Sonnet/Terra-class reviewer. A deep issue uses an Opus/Sol-class builder and an Opus/Sol-class reviewer. Thus 1 of the 2 supported issue-complexity paths currently reviews below the deep tier.

## Desired behavior

Keep builder sizing unchanged: standard issues build with Sonnet/Terra and deep issues build with Opus/Sol. Independently, launch every cross-review and re-review with Opus/Sol so the merge safety net does not share the cheaper builder tier's correlated blind spots.

## Key interfaces

Explore fresh; pointers, not line numbers.

- `Reviewer.review` is the policy seam: it currently accepts issue complexity and resolves the review model from it. Make the always-deep rule live here and simplify the interface if issue complexity is no longer meaningful to callers.
- The build/review/merge loop supplies issue complexity to initial reviews, revision reviews, and survivor re-reviews. Keep using that value for builders and revisers; do not accidentally promote build sessions.
- Claude and Codex runner adapters already own the deep-tier-to-model mapping. Reuse that mapping rather than hardcoding concrete model names in review orchestration.
- Amend the accepted sizing documentation and domain glossary so they distinguish the issue-sized builder dial from the always-deep reviewer policy.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A `standard` issue still launches its builder at `standard` complexity.
- [ ] A review for a `standard` issue launches at `deep` complexity.
- [ ] A review for a `deep` issue launches at `deep` complexity.
- [ ] Initial review, review after revision, and autonomous-survivor re-review all inherit the same always-deep policy from the Reviewer interface.
- [ ] The Reviewer interface no longer requires callers to provide issue complexity if that input has no remaining behavioral meaning.
- [ ] The sizing decision records and `CONTEXT.md` state that builder complexity is issue-sized while every reviewer uses the deep tier.
- [ ] A regression test exercises review through the public Reviewer interface and fails if a standard issue can cause `standard` to be passed to the reviewer runner again.
- [ ] `uv run pytest -q` passes.

## Out of scope

- Do not change intake's `standard | deep` complexity dial.
- Do not promote builders, revisers, intake sessions, responders, or other agent sessions to deep as part of this issue.
- Do not change pool selection, cross-tool independence, merge policy, revision limits, or UI evidence gates.
- Do not add model-specific branching outside the existing runner adapters.
- Do not build fleet cost accounting or attempt to validate the supplied ciq incident history without an authorized data source.

<!-- agentflow:original-below -->
<details>
<summary>Original issue as filed</summary>

## Context

The reviewer is currently sized by the **issue's** complexity dial: a `standard` issue gets a Sonnet/Terra builder AND a Sonnet/Terra-class reviewer. Exactly where the builder is cheapest, the safety net is too — and their blind spots correlate, which undercuts what cross-review exists for ("green CI but confidently wrong").

Field evidence (ciq-autotune): the jargon PR bodies, the misread "Clean — nothing flagged" headline bug (#337/#351), and the reviewer waiving the screenshot gate (#352) all cluster on standard-tier quick-wins; deep grilled issues produced charter-grade output.

Cost consideration: review sessions are short relative to builds, so always-deep review spends a modest slice of Opus/Sol headroom per PR — but it is per-PR, fleet-wide.

This is a settle-it-once dial decision (it amends ADR 0014/0018's sizing story), so it's held for the maintainer rather than self-scoped.

</details>

entries.title: mockup phase: daemon autonomously produces variant mockups on needs-mockup issues
entries.body:
> *agentflow intake — generated by AI.*

## Summary

Give the daemon a **mockup-production phase** so a parked UI issue advances on its own. Today intake correctly parks a UI issue at `needs-mockup`, but nothing ever draws the mockup — it sits until a human runs `/agentflow pickup` or replies out of nowhere. The maintainer picked the autonomous route: the daemon generates 3–4 wildly-different variants, posts their screenshots on the issue, and the maintainer picks (or asks for a tweak) in **one GitHub reply**, which locks the spec and lets the build proceed. Nobody enters an agent session.

## Verified

The premise holds against the code. The daemon's per-repo pass (`pipeline_once`) runs exactly four phases — triage, build, answer-a-parked-PR, re-rebase-survivors — and **none of them produces a mockup**. The only way a `needs-mockup` issue leaves that state is `_next_resumable_issue`, which fires **only after a maintainer comment** (a waiver or a pasted spec), or a hand-run pickup. So an untouched mockup issue has no automatic path forward — matching the filed report that the mockup queue (three issues in ciq-autotune since 07-08) has produced **zero** mockups since enrollment.

## Current behavior

- Intake parks a UI issue at `agentflow:needs-mockup` and pings once.
- The daemon then ignores it every cycle unless a maintainer comments.
- Result: the mockup phase exists on paper and stalls in practice — the worst of both worlds the maintainer called out.

## Desired behavior

- A new pipeline phase picks up the next `needs-mockup` issue that has **no agentflow mockup comment yet and no pending maintainer reply**, and spawns a session that runs the `/ui-mockups` skill headless for the declared surface.
- That session produces 3–4 **wildly-different** variants, screenshots each, and posts **one** comment on the *issue* embedding the screenshots, naming the variants (A–D) with a one-line description each, and asking the maintainer to reply with a pick or an adjustment. The variant HTML is preserved (committed to a branch), not left to die in an ephemeral worktree.
- The issue stays `needs-mockup`. When the maintainer replies with a pick, the existing resume path resolves it: it reads the mockup comment + the pick, **locks the chosen variant as a committed visual-spec file**, and promotes the issue to `ready-for-agent` with the locked spec referenced in the brief — so the eventual build has a real mockup to match (charter: locked *before* implemented).
- One variant round per issue is enough to unblock; a request for a *different* set is a follow-up reply the resume path handles, not an infinite auto-loop.

## Key interfaces

*Explore fresh — pointers, not line numbers.*

- **The pipeline pass** (`agentflow/loop.py`, `pipeline_once`): add the produce phase here alongside `intake_once` / `run_once` / `respond_once` / `recheck_once`. Model it on `respond_once`: find the next eligible issue, guard on pool headroom (`pick_pair`), claim it, spawn a session in a worktree, return a one-line result.
- **Dispatch dedup / claim label**: mirror the `BUILDING` / `TRIAGING` claim pattern (`_claim` / `_release`) with a new mockup-in-progress claim so a concurrent or next cycle skips an issue already being drawn. A crash before release should be a fail-safe skip, not a double-draw.
- **The produce session prompt**: like `RESPOND_PROMPT` / `BUILD_PROMPT` — invoke `/ui-mockups` for the repo's `ui_surfaces`, require headless screenshots, commit+push the variants, and post the issue comment.
- **TRAP — the marker**: the produce comment MUST contain `INTAKE_MARK` ("agentflow intake") so `awaiting_recheck` / `replies_since_intake` treat it as *ours*, not as a maintainer reply. Miss this and the daemon's own mockup comment instantly reads as a maintainer answer and the resume path fires on itself. All agentflow comments are authored by the maintainer's own `gh` account — the marker prefix is the only thing distinguishing them.
- **TRAP — teaching the resume path the pick**: intake's resume (`intake.py` `intake(..., extra=)`, and its prompt) currently understands a *waiver* or a *pasted spec*. A **variant pick** ("B", "the second one", "A but tighter") is a new reply shape — intake must fetch the mockup comment, map the pick to a variant, and lock that variant's file as the spec before promoting to ready.
- **TRAP — locked-before-built (ADR 0018)**: the build's UI-evidence gate (`gate.py`) parks any UI PR whose screenshots don't match *the locked mockup*. So the locked spec has to be a committed file the build can match against — not just a screenshot embedded in the brief. On a `reviewed`/`guarded` repo, locking that file is a human one-click merge of a small mockup PR (still no agent session); on `autonomous`, it can land on its own. Honor the repo profile the same way the build/merge path does.
- **Read-only data pull**: this repo declares no real-data snapshot; the ciq-autotune counts are the maintainer's own framing and are corroborated by the code having no produce phase.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `pipeline_once` gains a mockup-production phase; its one-line result appears in the daemon's per-cycle log next to intake/build/respond/recheck.
- [ ] The phase selects the next `needs-mockup` issue that has **no agentflow mockup comment yet** and **no pending maintainer reply**, respecting pool headroom and a mockup-in-progress claim (no double-draw across cycles).
- [ ] The produce session posts exactly **one** issue comment carrying `INTAKE_MARK`, embedding 3–4 variant screenshots with a one-line description each and a clear "reply to pick or adjust" ask; the variant HTML is committed to a branch, not lost with the worktree.
- [ ] After the produce comment, `awaiting_recheck` returns **False** on that issue (the daemon does not treat its own comment as a maintainer reply); it returns **True** only once the maintainer actually replies.
- [ ] A maintainer pick reply promotes the issue to `ready-for-agent`, drops `needs-mockup`, and the resulting brief references the **locked, committed** chosen variant so the build's UI-evidence gate has a mockup to match.
- [ ] Regression test (would have failed before this change): a `needs-mockup` issue with only intake's park comment is picked up by the new phase and yields an `INTAKE_MARK`-carrying mockup comment; and a second test asserting that immediately after that comment `awaiting_recheck([...]) is False` (the self-trigger guard). Both through the public phase/pure-helper interfaces, not internals.
- [ ] `uv run pytest -q` is green.

## Out of scope

- No change to the `/ui-mockups` skill itself — the daemon *drives* it, it already runs headless.
- No auto-approval of the maintainer's pick: the daemon never chooses the variant, and never merges a mockup PR on a `reviewed`/`guarded` repo — a human still clicks merge to lock the spec there.
- No infinite re-draw: one variant round per issue; a request for a fresh set is an ordinary follow-up reply, not an auto-loop.
- No dashboard/UI surface change in this issue — this is daemon/pipeline plumbing (the produced mockups are posted to GitHub, not rendered in the app).

<!-- agentflow:original-below -->
<details>
<summary>Original issue as filed</summary>

## Context

Intake correctly parks UI issues at `needs-mockup`, but nothing ever advances them — since enrollment, the mockup queue in ciq-autotune (#276, #277, #332) has produced **zero** mockups. The `/ui-mockups` skill already runs headless (multiple variants, screenshots, iterate-to-locked-spec), so the open question is who drives it: the daemon, or only a human via `pickup`.

The goal tension: the maintainer wants mockup phases AND minimal time in agent sessions. Today the mockup phase exists on paper and stalls in practice — the worst of both.

This is a product/autonomy decision (which stage the daemon may run unattended), so it's held for the maintainer rather than self-scoped.

</details>

entries.title: manual dispatch: bypass recent-session guard while preserving spend ceilings
entries.body:
### Problem

When I drive a build by hand — `/agentflow build <N>` from an active Claude Code session — it almost always defers with:

```
#N: no pool has headroom right now — deferring
```

but the pools aren't actually out of headroom. In the case that prompted this, Claude was at 19% of peak and Codex at 24% of limit — both wide open. The real cause is the dispatch gate's *"a session was active in the last 10m"* guard tripping on **my own** interactive session. Because I'm sitting at the keyboard running the command, the guard sees recent session activity and blocks — so the one time I most want a build to fire (I explicitly asked for it), it's the one time it can't.

That guard exists to stop the **unattended daemon** from eating the usage window out from under a live session. That rationale is correct for the daemon. It's exactly backwards for a by-hand `build`: the operator *is* the live session, and they're explicitly requesting the dispatch.

### Current behavior

`build_issue` → `_dispatch_build` calls `pick_pair()`, the same call the daemon's `run_once` uses. `pick_pair` → `balancer._query_pool` runs `triage-gate.sh check`, whose gate 1 blocks when any transcript was written in the last `ACTIVE_WINDOW_MIN` (10m) minutes. An operator running `/agentflow build` is, by definition, recent activity — so the operator-initiated path inherits a guard meant only for unattended dispatch and defers.

### Desired behavior

An operator-initiated `build <N>` (and by-hand intake, same shape) should **skip the "recently active session" guard** while still respecting the real spend / rate-limit ceiling. If the pool is genuinely rate-limited (spend over threshold), still defer and say so — that guard stays. Only the recent-activity block is bypassed for an explicit by-hand request. The daemon's `run_once` path is unchanged and keeps the full guard.

### Key interfaces (explore fresh; pointers, not line numbers)

- `agentflow/loop.py` — `build_issue` / `_dispatch_build` (by-hand) vs `run_once` (daemon), both funnel through the same `pick_pair()`. The operator-initiated signal has to reach the balancer from here.
- `agentflow/balancer.py` — `pick_pair` / `_query_pool` / `choose_pair`. `_query_pool` already runs `spend` (real %) separately from `check` (clear/busy incl. the activity block); note that `choose_pair`/`parse_pct` are the pure test surface and should stay pure.
- `~/Code/ConnorGriffin/dotfiles/scripts/triage-gate.sh` — gate 1 is the recent-activity block (`ACTIVE_WINDOW_MIN`); gate 2 is spend/rate-limit. The two are already separable; prefer signaling "ignore activity, keep spend" over duplicating the threshold logic in Python (one source of truth for the ceiling).
- **Trap:** don't bypass the spend ceiling — a by-hand build must still defer when the pool is actually rate-limited.
- **Trap:** in single-tool fallback (only one pool clear), the caller must still not auto-merge (ADR 0003) — bypassing the activity guard must not quietly change the pair-vs-single decision.

### Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `build_issue` invoked while an interactive session is active (transcript written < 10m ago) dispatches instead of deferring, as long as spend is under threshold.
- [ ] A by-hand build against a genuinely rate-limited pool still defers with a clear message (spend ceiling honored).
- [ ] The daemon's `run_once` dispatch path still respects the full activity guard — unattended dispatch behavior is unchanged.
- [ ] A test through the balancer interface that fails if an operator-initiated dispatch is blocked solely by the recent-activity guard.

### Out of scope

- Changing the activity window length or the spend threshold values.
- Any change to auto-merge / park behavior beyond preserving the existing single-tool rule.

entries.title: daemon/dashboard: serve the dashboard and report dispatch state
entries.body:
> *agentflow intake — generated by AI.*

## Agent Brief

**Summary**

Run the operator dashboard inside the supervised daemon and truthfully report whether dispatch is enabled. Preserve standalone dashboard launch for development and implement the maintainer-selected Variant B compact disclosure.

**Verified**

- `agentflow.daemon.main()` acquires the single-instance lock, starts exactly 1 heartbeat thread, performs startup recovery, and enters the blocking poll loop. It starts 0 HTTP servers.
- `agentflow.server.main()` is currently a separate command that binds 1 `ThreadingHTTPServer` to `127.0.0.1`; `AGENTFLOW_DASH_PORT` defaults to `8787`.
- `agentflow.dashboard_data.snapshot()` currently returns exactly 2 top-level fields, `pools` and `repos`. It always queries 2 pools, and the daemon currently enrolls 6 repositories, but the snapshot contains no enabled/dormant dispatch state.
- The accepted persistent-orchestrator design says 1 supervised service owns both dispatch and the dashboard API, so the reported split is real and contradicts the intended operating model.
- The maintainer selected Variant B. The locked visual spec is `mockups/dashboard-daemon-pill.html` on branch `agentflow/codex/mockup-44-daemon-dashboard-serve-the-operator-dash` at commit `1cffad81855284913d30dbb5f1b7e3ae92bf98c8`.

**Current behavior**

A normal daemon launch starts the 1 polling process and its heartbeat but leaves port `8787` unserved. A second command, `python -m agentflow.server`, is required to start the dashboard. The page refreshes its snapshot every `15,000` ms, but that snapshot cannot distinguish an enabled fleet from a live-but-dormant daemon.

**Desired behavior**

A normal supervised daemon launch should own both the polling loop and a background dashboard server in the same process. The dashboard must remain available when the global enable flag is absent and must show that the console is live while dispatch is dormant. Its state should update from the same enable-flag truth used by the polling loop, without restarting either service. Port configuration remains `AGENTFLOW_DASH_PORT`, default `8787`, and standalone dashboard launch remains available for development. `--once` remains a finite one-cycle command rather than becoming a persistent server.

**Key interfaces**

Explore fresh; pointers, not line numbers:

- `agentflow.daemon.main()` — owns the lock, heartbeat, startup recovery, `--once`, and polling lifecycle. Dashboard startup and shutdown must preserve those guarantees.
- The dashboard server construction and `Handler` — provide a reusable server lifecycle while retaining the standalone `main()` entry point and loopback binding.
- `agentflow.dashboard_data.snapshot()` and `/api/snapshot` — expose live enabled/dormant dispatch truth through the public snapshot interface.
- The shipping dashboard renderer — implement the compact status pill and disclosure from the locked Variant B spec using live snapshot data.
- Trap: the server currently imports `REPOS` from the daemon. Importing the server back into the daemon would create a circular dependency; establish ownership or inject dependencies without duplicating the repository list.
- Trap: Variant B contains mock-only variant links and an enabled/dormant toggle. Those review controls are not part of the product and must not ship.
- Trap: dispatch state must be evaluated live, not captured only at process startup, because adding or removing the enable flag must be reflected without a restart.

**Acceptance criteria**

- [ ] Running `python -m agentflow.daemon` starts both normal pipeline polling and an HTTP dashboard listener in the same process.
- [ ] The listener binds to `127.0.0.1`, defaults to port `8787`, and honors `AGENTFLOW_DASH_PORT`.
- [ ] With the enable flag absent, `/api/snapshot` still responds and identifies dispatch as dormant; the daemon claims no new work.
- [ ] Adding or removing the enable flag changes the reported dispatch state without restarting the daemon or dashboard.
- [ ] The shipping dashboard matches locked Variant B: a compact labelled status pill opens an accessible disclosure separating “console live” from “dispatch enabled/dormant.”
- [ ] No mock-only variant picker or manual state toggle ships.
- [ ] `python -m agentflow.server` remains a supported standalone development command.
- [ ] `python -m agentflow.daemon --once` still performs exactly 1 recovery-and-cycle pass and exits without leaving a dashboard service alive.
- [ ] A regression test exercises the daemon through its public entry point and proves that `/api/snapshot` becomes reachable without separately starting `agentflow.server`; it would fail if the original split-process bug returned.
- [ ] Tests cover both enabled and dormant snapshot states through the HTTP interface.
- [ ] The PR includes before/after Playwright screenshots demonstrating that the implementation matches the locked Variant B file.
- [ ] `uv run pytest -q` passes.

**Out of scope**

- Dashboard controls that create or remove the enable flag.
- Per-pool or per-repository pause controls.
- A second managed process or LaunchAgent.
- Binding the dashboard beyond loopback or adding authentication/network exposure.
- Removing the standalone development server.
- Changing the daemon poll interval, enrolled repository list, or unrelated dashboard data.

<!-- agentflow:original-below -->
<details>
<summary>Original issue as filed</summary>

## What
The LaunchAgent only runs the pipeline daemon (`python -m agentflow.daemon`). The dashboard (`python -m agentflow.server`, http://localhost:8787) is a separate process you have to start by hand — so after a machine restart or a daemon restart, the fleet keeps running but the web UI is silently down until someone remembers to launch it manually.

## Why it matters
The dashboard is the only at-a-glance view of what the fleet is doing. Today it can be down without any signal — you only notice when you go looking for it and the port is dead. The thing that watches the fleet shouldn't be the thing most likely to be missing.

## What we want
Starting the daemon should also bring up the web UI, so a single launch (the LaunchAgent, a restart, boot) gives you both the running pipeline and a live dashboard on 8787. One process to own, one thing to keep alive.

## Notes / things to check
- The dashboard already runs in its own `ThreadingHTTPServer`; the daemon loop is a blocking `while True` sleep loop. Combining them means the UI runs alongside the loop (e.g. the server in a background thread) rather than as a second managed process.
- Port stays configurable via `AGENTFLOW_DASH_PORT` (default 8787).
- Keep the kill switch honest: the dashboard should reflect the dormant state, not imply the fleet is working when the enable flag is gone.
- Decide whether the dashboard should still be launchable standalone (useful for dev) even when bundled into the daemon.

Found while investigating why the UI looked down — the daemon was up but nothing was serving 8787.

</details>

entries.title: merge pipeline: rebase and recheck parked PRs after main advances
entries.body:
## Summary

When one PR merges, `main` moves — and every other open agentflow PR that was
parked clean can silently become `CONFLICTING`. Nothing re-rebases those
survivors, so a batch of sibling PRs pile up: the first merges fine and the rest
are only discovered to be conflicted by hand, at merge time, with no signal on
the PR. [ADR 0009](docs/adr/0009-collision-safety.md) **specifies** this floor
(step 2: "each surviving sibling re-rebases and reruns CI against the new
`main`") but nothing implements it.

## Verified

- Field evidence: a recent batch of agentflow sibling PRs all parked clean off
  the same `main`; as each was merged, the next went `CONFLICTING`. No comment
  was ever posted on a survivor — so #18's comment-driven responder would not
  have woken on any of them.
- The per-cycle work (`loop.pipeline_once`) is one intake + one build. Once
  `_build_review_merge` parks a PR and returns, no cycle re-enters it; the
  originating issue is treated as in-flight (`_issues_in_flight`) while the PR is
  open, so neither the PR nor the issue is ever touched again.
- This is distinct from #18. #18 is **reactive** — it wakes on a *maintainer
  comment*. This is **proactive** — the trigger is *a sibling merged and `main`
  moved*, with no comment involved.

## Desired behavior

Each daemon cycle, for every open agentflow PR whose base has advanced since the
branch last rebased: rebase the branch onto `origin/main` and rerun CI, then
route by the repo's `profile:`:

- **autonomous** — on a clean rebase + green CI, the PR stays eligible; on
  conflict (or a post-rebase CI break not the PR's own), auto-revise up to the
  usual budget, then park-and-ping. Serialize merges so only one lands per cycle
  and survivors re-rebase against the new `main` before the next is eligible.
- **reviewed / guarded** — never merge; on conflict, park-and-ping so a
  conflicted survivor is never silent. A clean re-rebase just keeps the PR
  mergeable for the human.

Reuse the revise contract: same branch, never a new PR, never a merge on a
human-merge repo.

## Key interfaces

The park/merge machinery in `agentflow/loop.py` (`_build_review_merge`, the
revise pass) and `agentflow/gate.py`; the same-branch push discipline used by
`/agentflow revise`. Traps: don't churn a PR whose base has *not* moved (compare
merge-base, don't blind-rebase every cycle); don't wake on our own park/revise
comments; a rebase that touches nothing should be a no-op, not a force-push.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] After a merge advances `main`, an open sibling PR that now conflicts is
      re-rebased within one cycle and, if still conflicting, parked-and-pinged —
      not left silent.
- [ ] A survivor whose base has not moved is left untouched (no needless
      force-push) — pure predicate test on "base advanced since last rebase".
- [ ] `autonomous`: merges serialize — one PR lands per cycle, survivors
      re-rebase + rerun CI before the next is eligible.
- [ ] The pass never opens a new PR and never merges on a `reviewed`/`guarded`
      repo.

## Out of scope

Answering maintainer comments on parked PRs (that is #18). Upfront intake
overlap-prediction to avoid fanning out conflicting siblings (ADR 0009 marks it
an off-by-default optimization).

entries.title: Daemon logging: report route starts and per-pool block reasons
entries.body:
## Problem

The daemon logs one terminal line per repo per cycle, so an active dispatch is invisible and a deferral never says *why* it's blocked.

Concretely, this cycle logged:

```
agentflow: ConnorGriffin/homelab: intake: #1: no pool has headroom for intake — deferring · build: #9: no pool has headroom right now — deferring
```

`homelab` was deferred because Codex was busy running agentflow's *own* intake sessions on #44 and #45 — but nothing in the log said so. The only way to discover the occupant was to inspect the running worktrees by hand.

The root cause is that each cycle only surfaces two states:

- a **deferral** ("no pool has headroom") — when it can't dispatch, or
- a **completed outcome** ("#44: scoped to ready") — logged only after the blocking session finishes.

The moment an issue is actually routed to an agent — and the whole minutes-long session that follows — is logged silently between those two states.

## What to add

1. **A dispatch-start log line.** When a builder is picked, emit something like `#44: routing → codex (intake)` so an in-progress route is visible the instant it starts, not only when it lands.

2. **Name the occupant in the deferral.** When a pool has no headroom, say which tool is busy and why, e.g. `no pool has headroom (codex busy, claude: you) — deferring`. The pool picker already computes each pool's block reason, so the information exists — it's just discarded.

Together these turn a bare "no headroom" into an actionable "Codex is mid-build on #44, Claude is your live session."

## Notes

- Not a capacity bug — the pools behave correctly; this is purely observability.
- Related: the underlying stale-rate-limit gate bug (a Codex window that had already reset kept reporting its old percent) was fixed separately in the dotfiles `triage-gate.sh`.

entries.title: activity guard: don't count agentflow's own ephemeral worktree sessions as operator activity
entries.body:
## What happened

After agentflow completed an unattended Claude intake session, its next scheduler check reported that Claude had been active within the last 10 minutes and withheld the pool. No operator had used Claude for hours, and Claude was at only 17% of its trailing five-hour spend.

The activity was agentflow's own ephemeral hand. Its transcript was updated at 1:28 PM and the same failure reproduced after another unattended intake transcript was updated at 1:39 PM. The live gate then returned:

```text
blocked: a session was active in the last 10m
spend: trailing-5h spend at 17% of peak
```

This can defer queued work entirely when Codex is genuinely in interactive use, or unnecessarily force single-pool routing despite ample Claude headroom.

## What I expected

The recent-activity guard should reserve pool capacity for human interactive sessions. Sessions spawned by agentflow's own ephemeral hands should not make the orchestrator treat that pool as operator-busy.

Real operator activity and rate-limit ceilings must continue to defer unattended work.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Enable the daemon with a queued issue that dispatches an unattended Claude intake, build, or review.
2. Let that ephemeral hand finish and write its Claude transcript.
3. Within 10 minutes, let the scheduler evaluate another queued item.
4. Observe that Claude is marked unavailable because of recent session activity, even though the only recent Claude session was spawned by agentflow itself and spend remains below the reserve threshold.

## Additional context

Captured on July 11, 2026 while processing homelab issue #11. The recent transcripts identified themselves as agentflow Claude intake worktrees. The dashboard simultaneously showed 83% Claude headroom and no in-flight PR, while ready homelab work remained queued.

Current tests cover the distinction between unattended daemon dispatch and explicit by-hand dispatch using generic recent activity, but do not cover self-generated ephemeral-hand transcripts.

entries.body:
> *agentflow intake — generated by AI.*

**Summary**

Make worktrees truly session-scoped: remove each safely disposable working copy after its result is durable, recover old owned leftovers without touching recoverable or foreign work, and add `.agentflow/` to repository ignore rules during explicit enrollment.

**Verified**

`_WorktreeRunner.build`, `Intake.intake`, `Reviewer.review`, `produce_once`, `_checkout_pr_branch`, and `_rebase_branch` create or reuse working copies but do not remove them when their sessions finish. `prune_stale_worktrees` is the only cleanup path: `pipeline_once` calls it for the `claude` and `codex` builder roots, and it removes only clean directories whose derived `agentflow/{tool}/{directory}` branch has a merged or closed PR. It does not cover intake, review, mockup, response, rebase, open-PR builds, legacy branch names, or stale Git registrations, and it never runs `git worktree prune`.

A fresh read-only check of homelab still finds **9 leaf directories using 1.3 GB** under `.agentflow/worktrees/`. **Eight** are clean homelab-owned completed sessions: four intake copies for issues 1, 6, and 11; reviews for merged PRs 16 and 17; and legacy builds for merged PRs 19 and 20. The ninth is a clean but foreign dotfiles worktree backing open PR 18. Physical containment therefore does not establish ownership. Homelab still reports `?? .agentflow/` because its ignore rules contain no `.agentflow/` entry.

Agentflow itself currently has **29 leaf directories using 259 MB** and **30 registered worktrees including its main checkout**. `enroll_repo` in the enrollment script wires instruction files and migrates labels but never updates `.gitignore`.

**Current behavior**

Completed intake and review sessions remain registered indefinitely. Builds can be removed later only when they use the current branch convention and their PR has closed or merged; an open PR retains its build copy even after the build session has ended. Legacy builds such as homelab PRs 19 and 20 evade the derived branch lookup. Mockup, response, and rebase sessions have no cleanup path. Enrollment leaves agentflow state visible to `git status`.

**Desired behavior**

After an intake, review, build, mockup, response, or rebase session records or pushes its durable result, its clean and safely disposable worktree is removed—even when the associated PR remains open. Failures that contain dirty files, unpushed commits, or otherwise recoverable progress remain available for recovery.

On daemon startup, and safely on later recovery passes, prune stale Git registrations and remove completed agentflow-owned worktrees across current and recognized legacy naming. Determine ownership from Git worktree/repository metadata rather than directory containment. Never remove another repository's worktree merely because it is nested beneath the target repository.

Explicit enrollment adds `.agentflow/` to the target repository's `.gitignore` exactly once. Re-running enrollment applies the protection to already-enrolled repositories; normal daemon cycles never edit repository ignore rules.

**Key interfaces**

Explore fresh; pointers, not line numbers.

- The shared runner worktree choreography is the likely deep-module seam for safe removal after a launched session returns. Keep disposal policy concentrated rather than duplicating raw Git commands across lanes.
- Intake, reviewer, build/revise, mockup, response, and survivor-rebase boundaries identify when each session's result has become durable.
- The existing stale-worktree sweep and daemon startup/cycle entry points are the recovery path; broaden behavior without treating GitHub lookup failures as proof that work is disposable.
- Repository enrollment must retain its current dry-run, non-destructive, and idempotent behavior while editing existing ignore files without disturbing unrelated entries.
- Traps: physical nesting is not ownership; a clean status does not prove commits were pushed; legacy branches do not follow the current `agentflow/{tool}/issue-*` convention; dirty or uncertain work must be retained and surfaced rather than force-removed.

**Acceptance criteria**

- [ ] Completed intake, review, build, mockup, response, and rebase sessions remove their own clean, safely disposable registered worktree after their result is durable.
- [ ] A build worktree is removed after it opens or updates an open PR; later response or rebase work recreates it on demand and removes it again when finished.
- [ ] Dirty worktrees, clean worktrees with unpushed/recoverable commits, active sessions, and worktrees whose state cannot be verified are retained.
- [ ] Startup/recovery runs `git worktree prune` and recognizes both current and verified legacy agentflow worktrees.
- [ ] Against the verified homelab snapshot, recovery identifies the **8** completed homelab-owned leaves as removable while retaining the nested dotfiles worktree for open PR **18**, reducing those **9** leaves to **1** without touching foreign work.
- [ ] Enrollment adds the exact `.agentflow/` ignore rule once to new and already-enrolled repositories; repeated enrollment produces no duplicate and preserves existing ignore content.
- [ ] Existing repositories receive the protection through an explicit one-time re-enrollment path; the daemon does not silently modify `.gitignore`.
- [ ] A regression test exercises cleanup through the public lifecycle interface across multiple sessions and fails if completed registrations accumulate or an in-flight/recoverable/foreign worktree is removed.
- [ ] Enrollment tests cover dry-run, apply, an absent `.gitignore`, an existing `.gitignore`, and repeated application.
- [ ] `uv run pytest -q` passes.

**Out of scope**

- Automatically deleting dirty work, unpushed commits, or state whose ownership/completion cannot be established.
- Removing the nested dotfiles worktree backing open PR 18 or any unrelated worktree outside agentflow ownership.
- Silently editing enrolled repositories during daemon polling.
- Changing branch naming, merge policy, or the user-facing dashboard.
